executive_thesis:
Composed at Paris between 1257 and 1259 and preserved in part in his own autograph, Thomas Aquinas's *Expositio super librum Boethii De Trinitate* (Questions V and VI) constitutes the most rigorous epistemological treatise of the Latin Middle Ages on the architecture and methodology of the theoretical sciences. Confronting competing Aristotelian, Boethian, Platonic, Avicennian, and Victorine classifications of human knowledge, Aquinas grounds the tripartite division of speculative philosophy—natural science, mathematics, and divine science—not in arbitrary ontological taxonomies, nor merely in subjective psychological faculties, but in the *per se* differences of speculative objects (*speculabilia*) precisely insofar as they stand proportioned to an immaterial intellect seeking necessary scientific truth. Because the intellect is immaterial in its power and demonstrative science (*scientia*) demands immobile necessity in its object, speculative objects are diversified essentially by their grade of removal from matter and motion: physics treats realities that depend upon sensible matter both in being (*secundum esse*) and in definition (*secundum intellectum*); mathematics treats realities that depend upon matter in being yet are defined without sensible matter; and divine science treats realities independent of matter and motion in being itself.

The analytical summit of this architecture appears in Question V, Article 3, where Aquinas justifies the truth and objectivity of mathematical abstraction by mapping Aristotle's twofold operation of the intellect (*On the Soul* III.6) onto the real structure of essence and existence. Whereas the intellect's second operation—composition and division, which regards a thing's very act of being (*ipsum esse*)—cannot truly disjoin what is united in reality and therefore exercises *separatio* only where realities can actually subsist apart from matter (the domain of metaphysics), the first operation—the *understanding of indivisibles*, which regards quidditative nature—can truthfully consider apart what is conjoined in reality whenever the intelligible account (*ratio*) of one principle does not depend upon another. Within this first operation Aquinas distinguishes two irreducible modes of abstraction: *abstraction of the whole* (*abstractio totius*), whereby a universal specific nature such as man is abstracted from *designated matter* (*materia signata*) while retaining common sensible matter (the procedure of natural philosophy and all sciences generally); and *abstraction of form* (*abstractio formae*), whereby the accidental form of dimensive quantity and figure is abstracted from *sensible matter* (tactile and visual qualities and physical motion) while retaining *intelligible matter* (*materia intelligibilis*), namely substance apprehended solely by the intellect as the underlying subject of extension. Because accidents accrue to substance in an ontological order wherein dimensive quantity precedes sensible qualities and motion, and because quantity carries position (*situs*, the order of parts) as a constitutive difference within its own notion, the geometer abstracts without mendacity while retaining the numerical plurality of congruent figures—such as several equal straight lines or several equilateral triangles—required for geometric construction and demonstration.

Question VI completes this ontological division with a corresponding methodology of cognitive procedure and judgmental verification. In Article 1, Aquinas pairs natural philosophy with proceeding *rationally* (*rationabiliter*, moving discursively from sensible effects to extrinsic causes), mathematics with proceeding *disciplinably* (*disciplinaliter*, demonstrating with supreme certitude and pedagogical clarity through intrinsic formal causality alone), and metaphysics with proceeding *intellectually* (*intellectualiter*, gathering multiplicity into unity at the ultimate term of causal and formal *resolutio*). In Article 2, Aquinas establishes his decisive noetic distinction between the *beginning* (*principium*) of human cognition in apprehension and its *term* (*terminus*) in judgment. While all human thought in the present life originates in sense and relies upon the *phantasm* (*phantasma*) as a permanent foundation, judgment does not terminate uniformly across the three sciences: physical judgment terminates at external sense; metaphysical judgment uses phantasms via causality, transcendence, and negation without ever terminating at sense or imagination; and mathematical judgment uniquely *terminates at the imagination* (*terminari ad imaginationem*). Liberated from sensible perturbations yet anchored in imaginable dimensive extension, mathematical judgment attains exact geometric truths—such as a straight line touching a sphere at a single indivisible point—that surpass sensory perception while finding faithful structural verification in constructive spatial intuition.

conceptual_table.significance: The formal object of theoretical intellect, whose *per se* differences arise from combining the immateriality of the intellective power with the immobile necessity required by scientific habit (*scientia*), yielding the three grades of removal from matter and motion.

Matter considered under determinate spatial and temporal dimensions (*hic et nunc*, this flesh and these bones), which serves as the principle of individuation and singular mobility and is left behind by every universal science.

Corporeal matter endowed with sensible qualities (hot, cold, colored, heavy, mobile), retained universally in natural definitions (flesh and bones in general) through *abstraction of the whole*, but excluded from mathematical definitions through *abstraction of form*.

Substance considered prior to sensible qualities solely as the subject underlying dimensive quantity, together with the homogeneous parts of continuous extension itself; comprehensible by the intellect and represented in pure spatial imagination, grounding both numerical multiplicity and material-part demonstrations in geometry.

conceptual_table.latin_term: Intelligentia indivisibilium vs. compositio et divisio
conceptual_table.english_term: Understanding of indivisibles vs. composition and division
conceptual_table.significance: The twofold operation of the intellect from *On the Soul* III.6: simple apprehension grasps quidditative essence (*quid est*), permitting truthful non-assertoric abstraction of conjoined realities, whereas judgment affirms or denies *ipsum esse* and therefore requires real separability whenever it disjoins.

Abstraction of a universal essential whole from accidental and designated material parts (the universal from the particular), corresponding to the union of whole and part; proper to natural philosophy and shared by all sciences.

Abstraction of the accidental form of quantity and figure from sensible matter while retaining *intelligible matter*, grounded in the ontological priority of dimensive quantity over sensible quality and motion in corporeal substance; proper to mathematics.

The negative judgment of the intellect's second operation declaring that one reality does not depend upon matter and motion in its very act of being (*secundum esse*), whether positively (God and angels) or neutrally (common being, substance, potency, and act); proper to metaphysics.

A constitutive difference intrinsic to dimensive quantity consisting in the order of parts in the continuum, enabling the geometer to imagine and number multiple congruent lines or equilateral triangles of a single species even after sensible matter has been abstracted.

Disciplines such as astronomy, harmonics (music), optics, mechanics, and the moving sphere that apply formal mathematical principles to sensible natural subjects, remaining formally akin to mathematics because their middle terms of demonstration are quantitative.

conceptual_table.english_term: Rationally, disciplinably (by way of learning), intellectually
conceptual_table.significance: The three cognitive modes appropriated respectively to physics (discursive reasoning from sensible effects to extrinsic causes), mathematics (demonstrative certitude via intrinsic formal causes and imaginable figures), and divine science (synthetic intellectual unity at the term of causal and formal resolution).

The verification of mathematical judgment in constructive spatial imagination rather than external sense or pure imageless intellection, anchored by the *phantasm* (*phantasma*) functioning as a permanent foundation in which exact quantitative relations are inspected.

section_summaries.heading: Question V, Article 1 — Division of Speculative Science
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Ten objections challenge the Boethian and Aristotelian division of theoretical philosophy into physics, mathematics, and theology. They argue successively from Aristotle's three intellectual virtues in *Ethics* VI (wisdom, science, understanding), Augustine's inclusion of logic within contemplative philosophy, the medieval curriculum of the seven liberal arts (trivium and quadrivium), the presence of theoretical divisions within operative arts like medicine, the apparent inclusion of mechanical and medical arts under physics, the impropriety of dividing metaphysics (whose universal subject is being) against particular sciences studying parts of being, alternative ontological divisions of being (potency and act, corporeal and incorporeal), and pedagogical versus foundational ordering.

In his *responsio* and ten replies, Aquinas first demarcates speculative from practical intellect by their respective ends (truth considered for its own sake versus truth ordered to productive or moral action) and corresponding matters (things not made by human work versus operable things). He then demonstrates that habits are differentiated not by accidental differences of things, but by *per se* differences of their formal objects: because the intellect is immaterial and scientific knowledge requires immobile necessity, *speculabilia* divide exhaustively into three grades of dependence upon matter in being and in understanding—yielding natural philosophy, mathematics, and divine science (no fourth combination being possible since understanding cannot depend on matter where being does not). The replies harmonize rival schemes by situating logic and the liberal arts as preparatory instruments (*organa*) possessing immediate *opera rationis*, distinguishing part-whole containment from subalternation (*propter quid* versus *quia*), isolating formal *ratio considerandi* in metaphysics, and reconciling metaphysical priority in itself with pedagogical posteriority *quoad nos* without circularity.
key_theses: Speculative intellect differs from practical intellect by its end—truth considered for itself—requiring objects not produced by human agency.
Habits and sciences are formally diversified only by *per se* differences of their objects as knowable, namely their degree of separation from matter and motion.

Speculative objects divide exhaustively into three orders: dependent on matter in being and understanding (physics), dependent in being but not understanding (mathematics), and independent in being (divine science).
Logic and the quadrivial liberal arts serve as propaedeutic pathways (*viae*) possessing immediate works of reason (*opera rationis*) such as syllogizing, numbering, and measuring.

Subalternated sciences (such as music under arithmetic or medicine under physics) receive their *propter quid* principles from higher theoretical sciences without compromising the speculative purity of the higher science.

section_summaries.heading: Question V, Article 2 — Natural Philosophy, Motion, and Designated Matter
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Seven objections question how a true demonstrative science of mobile and material things is possible at all: matter is the principle of individuation whereas science treats solely of universals; intellection inherently abstracts from matter; physics culminates in the immaterial First Mover; mobile things are contingent whereas science demands necessity; universals themselves do not move; physics investigates unmoved principles such as the soul, natural forms, and the earth at rest; and mutability extends to all creatures, including spiritual ones.

Aquinas diagnoses this aporia as the precise philosophical root of Plato's theory of separate Ideas: accepting Heraclitean flux in sensible particulars, Plato posited separate immobile substances to save scientific definition, failing to distinguish what belongs *per se* to the composite from what belongs *per accidens* to its intelligible form (*ratio*). Following *Metaphysics* VII, Aquinas shows that while the concrete composite (*this house*, *this man*) comes to be and moves *per se*, its essential nature (*ratio*) can be considered apart from the *hic et nunc* conditions of local motion and *designated matter* (*materia signata*, matter under determinate dimensions), while retaining *undesignated* or *common sensible matter* (flesh and bones in general). Considered in themselves in the intellect, these universal *rationes* are immobile foundations of necessary science; applied secondarily by *reflexio* through the lower sensitive powers, they yield genuine scientific knowledge of extramental mobile substances, while the First Mover enters physics only as the extrinsic causal *terminus* of motion—just as an indivisible point relates to a line as its endpoint without being a line.
key_theses: Plato posited separate Ideas because he failed to distinguish the *per se* generation and flux of the singular composite from the *per accidens* mutability of its intelligible form.

Natural philosophy abstracts the universal from the particular by leaving behind *designated matter* (*materia signata* under determinate dimensions) while retaining *common sensible matter* in its definitions.
Universal *rationes* are immobile according to their intellectual mode of consideration, yet serve as the formal media for knowing mobile, material realities outside the soul.
Scientific cognition attains singular mobile things secondarily through a *reflexio* aided by the lower sensitive powers.
The immaterial First Mover enters physics not as part of its subject-genus, but as its extrinsic causal limit (*terminus*), analogous to the point terminating a line.

section_summaries.heading: Question V, Article 3 — Mathematical Abstraction and Intelligible Matter
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Eight objections challenge the claim that mathematics considers material realities without matter and motion: considering material things without matter seems to violate truth as *adaequatio rei et intellectus*; every science must consider the parts of its subject, including matter; geometers number multiple straight lines of the same species to form triangles and squares, yet numerical multiplication within a species requires matter; geometry demonstrates via the material cause from quantitative parts (such as proving the angle in a semicircle right from two half-right angles); space measures motion; astronomy, mechanics, harmonics, and spherics study motion; astronomers and physicists prove shared conclusions like the earth's sphericity; and Ptolemy assigns incorruptible mobile spheres to mathematics.

In the celebrated five-part *responsio*, Aquinas distinguishes the intellect's first operation (*intelligentia indivisibilium*, apprehending quiddity) from its second operation (composition and division, judging *ipsum esse*). Because judgment asserts real existence or non-existence, it can truly disjoin only what is separable in reality (*separatio*, founding metaphysics). Simple apprehension, however, truthfully abstracts one conjoined reality from another whenever the essential *ratio* of the first does not depend upon the second, yielding two distinct abstractions: *abstraction of the whole* (*abstractio totius*, abstracting a specific nature from accidental *designated parts*, common to all sciences and characteristic of physics) and *abstraction of form* (*abstractio formae*, characteristic of mathematics). Because accidents supervene upon substance in an intrinsic order—dimensive quantity first, prior to sensible qualities and motion—quantity and figure depend in their intelligible essence not upon *sensible matter*, but solely upon *intelligible matter* (*materia intelligibilis*, substance grasped solely by the intellect as underlying extension, along with homogeneous quantitative parts). The replies vindicate *abstrahentium non est mendacium*, show that dimensive quantity carries *situs* (the order of parts) within its own notion to ground the imaginable multiplicity of congruent lines and equilateral triangles, assign part-whole geometric proofs to *intelligible matter*, and define *scientiae mediae* as formally mathematical applications of quantitative middle terms to natural subjects.
key_theses: The intellect's two operations—apprehension of essence and judgment of *esse*—ground a strict triad of epistemic distinctions: *separation* (metaphysics), *abstraction of form* (mathematics), and *abstraction of the whole* (physics).

Because dimensive quantity inheres in corporeal substance prior to sensible qualities and motion, mathematical forms can be truthfully understood without *sensible matter* (*abstrahentium non est mendacium*).
Mathematics does not abstract from all matter absolutely, but retains *intelligible matter*—substance as pure subject of extension and the homogeneous parts of continuous magnitude.
Dimensive quantity includes *situs* (the order of parts) as a constitutive difference, enabling the geometer to imagine numerically distinct congruent lines and figures within one species.
Intermediate sciences (*scientiae mediae*) such as astronomy and harmonics demonstrate conclusions about physical phenomena formally through abstract mathematical middle terms.

section_summaries.heading: Question V, Article 4 — Divine Science and Immaterial Separation
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Eight objections argue that divine science cannot treat realities wholly separated from matter and motion: human reason reaches God only through visible material effects (Romans 1); Scripture, Augustine, and Plato speak of divine wisdom or the First Mover as self-moving; angels move by choice and local mission and seem hylomorphically composed since they are not pure act; metaphysics studies *ens* and *substantia*, which encompass material beings, matter, and motion; metaphysics demonstrates through efficient and final causes, which imply motion; and revealed theology treats creation and human moral acts.

Aquinas resolves the question by analyzing the nature of principles. Unlike incomplete intrinsic principles (such as the unit of number or the point of a line, studied solely within the science of their principiates), universal causal principles of all beings are also complete, subsistent natures maximally in act, and therefore wholly free of matter and motion. Such divine realities admit a twofold theology: philosophical theology (metaphysics), whose proper subject is *ens in quantum est ens* and which reaches God and the separate Intelligences from sensible effects as the extrinsic principles of its subject; and the theology of Sacred Scripture, which receives divine self-revelation through faith and treats God himself directly as its proper subject. Crucially, Aquinas distinguishes two senses of separation from matter and motion *secundum esse*: positive immateriality, where a nature can never exist in matter (God and angels), and negative or neutral immateriality, where a ratio does not depend on matter in being and can exist either with or without matter (*ens*, *substantia*, *actus*, *potentia*). In the replies, Aquinas refutes universal hylomorphism by distinguishing act-potency composition (*esse* and *essentia*, *quo est* and *quod est*) in incorruptible angels from matter-form composition, and explains why metaphysics demonstrates via efficient and final causality whereas mathematics—abstracting only in thought—does not.
key_theses: Incomplete principles (such as unit and point) belong solely to the science of their principiates, whereas complete subsistent principles of all being admit both causal philosophical inquiry and self-revealing theological science.
Philosophical theology (metaphysics) has *being insofar as it is being* as its subject and treats God and separate substances as the universal principles of its subject.
Separation from matter *secundum esse* is twofold: positive exclusion of matter (God and angels) and ontological neutrality toward matter (*ens*, *substantia*, *potentia*, *actus*).
Created spiritual substances are free of hylomorphic matter-form composition, yet remain composed of essence (*quod est*) and received act of being (*quo est*, *ipsum esse*).

Unlike mathematical entities, which are separated only in consideration and therefore exclude efficient and final causes, metaphysical principles subsist in reality and exercise efficient and final causality.

section_summaries.heading: Question VI, Article 1 — The Ratiocinative, Disciplinary, and Intellectual Modes
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Organized as a triple disputation with twelve objections and six *sed contra* authorities, Question VI, Article 1 examines Boethius's appropriation of three cognitive modes to the three theoretical sciences: proceeding *rationally* (*rationabiliter*) in physics, *disciplinably* (*disciplinabiliter* / *disciplinaliter*) in mathematics, and *intellectually* (*intellectualiter*) in divine science. Regarding physics, Aquinas distinguishes three senses of a rational procedure: arguing from logical second intentions (*logica docens*, proper to logic and metaphysics as common sciences), arguing dialectically from probable premises (*logica utens*, preparatory in all sciences and characteristic of contingent moral inquiry), and following the native discursive rhythm of the rational soul—advancing from sensible signs and effects better known to us toward extrinsic causes better known by nature—which belongs preeminently to natural philosophy, in contrast to mathematics, which demonstrates solely through intrinsic formal definitions.

Regarding mathematics, Aquinas explains that proceeding *disciplinably*—by way of learning (*discere*), generating unshakable scientific conviction—belongs preeminently to mathematics because it occupies the epistemic golden mean between physics and theology: freed from the flux, variability, and multifactorial complexity of sensible matter (with arithmetic even simpler and more certain than geometry, which exists *ex additione*), yet directly accessible to sense and spatial imagination through phantasms of line, figure, and number, mathematics surpasses both natural and divine science in human certitude, just as Ptolemy observed in the *Almagest*. Regarding divine science, Aquinas contrasts discursive *ratio* (circling around multiplicity like circumference around center or time around eternity) with unifying *intellectus* (grasping multitude within one simple truth). Because all human reasoning terminates via *resolutio* either extrinsically at the supreme separate substances or intrinsically at *ens commune*, metaphysics stands closest to pure intellectual intuition, serving simultaneously as the last science learned by analytical *resolutio* and the *prima philosophia* supplying synthetic principles along the *via compositionis vel inventionis*.
key_theses: Natural philosophy proceeds *rationally* (*rationabiliter*) by mirroring the human soul's native discursive movement from sensible effects to ontologically distinct extrinsic causes.
Mathematics demonstrates purely through the formal cause; even when proving properties of a circle through a triangle, it actualizes figures potentially intrinsic to the quantitative continuum.
Mathematics proceeds *disciplinably* (*disciplinaliter*) with supreme human certitude because its objects are both immutable—unlike physical flux—and directly imaginable—unlike separate substances.
Logic must be learned before mathematics and the other sciences not because it is easier—being hardest as a science of second intentions—but because all sciences depend on its method.

Divine science proceeds *intellectually* (*intellectualiter*) as the ultimate *terminus* of both causal (extrinsic) and formal-universal (intrinsic) *resolutio*, gathering multiplicity into simple unity.

section_summaries.heading: Question VI, Article 2 — Phantasm and the Termination of Mathematical Judgment
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Six objections contend that even divine science must be led back to the imagination (*ad imaginationes deduci*): Sacred Scripture clothes divine truths in sensible metaphors; Aristotle teaches in *On the Soul* that the soul never understands without a *phantasm* (*phantasma*); Dionysius declares that the divine ray shines upon us only through sacred sensible veils; God is known from sensible effects; phantasms regulate our intellect as colors regulate sight; and cerebral injury impedes contemplation even of divine things. Counter-authorities from Dionysius's *Mystical Theology*, Augustine's *On the Trinity*, and Boethius's *Consolation* warn that reducing spiritual realities to corporeal images is the fountainhead of metaphysical error.

Aquinas resolves the tension by introducing a foundational epistemological distinction between the *beginning* (*principium*) of cognition, which pertains to apprehension, and its *term* (*terminus*), which pertains to judgment where truth is completed. In the present life, all human cognition begins in sense and depends continuously upon the *phantasm*—not as a transient ladder discarded after abstraction, but as a permanent foundation (*permanens ut quoddam fundamentum*) in which the intellect inspects its objects either positively or negatively. Yet the *terminus* where judgment is verified differs radically across the three sciences: in natural philosophy, judgment must *terminate at sense* (*terminari ad sensum*), conforming to sensory manifestation; in mathematics, because definitions abstract from *sensible matter* while retaining imaginable dimensive quantity, judgment must *terminate at the imagination* (*terminari ad imaginationem*) and not at sense—for a mathematical straight line touches a sphere at a single indivisible point, surpassing any sensible ruler and bronze sphere; and in divine science, judgment terminates neither at sense nor at the imagination, employing phantasms solely as starting points via Dionysian causality, transcendence, and negation. Methodological ruin ensues whenever thinkers attempt to apply a uniform criterion of verification across physics, mathematics, and metaphysics.
key_theses: Every human cognitive act must be analyzed according to both its *principium* (apprehension, originating in sense and phantasm) and its *terminus* (judgment, where truth is verified).
In the present state of life, the *phantasm* remains a permanent foundation (*permanens fundamentum*) of intellectual operation across all sciences, analogous to first principles in demonstration.
Physical judgment *terminates at sense* (*ad sensum*), because sensible qualities and motions belong intrinsically to the definitive nature of natural bodies.

Mathematical judgment *terminates at the imagination* (*ad imaginationem*) and surpasses sense, verifying exact geometric relations—such as point-tangency between line and sphere—in pure spatial intuition.

Metaphysical judgment terminates in the pure intellect alone, employing sense and imagination strictly as points of departure via causality, excess, and negation without ever judging divine things to be imaginable.

section_notes.heading: Commentary on Question V, Article 1
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas constructs his division of theoretical philosophy by synthesizing Boethius's *De Trinitate* (c. 2) with three canonical Aristotelian loci: *Metaphysics* VI.1 (1026a10–19), which establishes physics, mathematics, and theology according to separability and immobility; *Physics* II.2 (193b22–194b15), which contrasts the physicist's inclusion of sensible matter with the mathematician's consideration of surfaces, volumes, lines, and points apart from motion; and *Posterior Analytics* I.2 and I.7–13, which demand immobile necessity of scientific objects and govern the subalternation of *quia* sciences to *propter quid* sciences. Crucially, Aquinas enriches this Greek framework with Avicenna's *Liber de philosophia prima* (I.1–3) and *Canon medicinae* (I.1.1), refining the distinction between the ontological subject-genus (*ens commune*) and the formal *ratio considerandi*, while integrating Ptolemy's *Almagest* (I.1) and Hugh of Saint Victor's *Didascalicon* (III.3) to situate logic and the quadrivium cleanly as methodological propaedeutics.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: In replying to the third objection (*ad 3*), Aquinas characterizes geometry and arithmetic within the quadrivium as liberal arts because they exercise an immediate *opus rationis*—numbering and measuring—within pure reason itself. This directly illuminates the dual propositional structure of Euclid's *Elements*, traditionally divided since Proclus into *theorems* (demonstrating eternal properties of figures) and *problems* (constructing figures from postulates, such as bisecting an angle or constructing an equilateral triangle in *Elements* I.1 and a square in *Elements* I.46). Unlike mechanical arts that manipulate recalcitrant physical timber or bronze, Euclidean straightedge-and-compass postulates enact an interior rational construction whose intelligibility depends neither on sensible matter nor on physical force, while subalternating applied optical, harmonic, and astronomical treatises (*Optics*, *Sectio Canonis*, *Phaenomena*) by supplying their *propter quid* quantitative demonstrations.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In Chapter VII of *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954), Peter Hoenen S.J. singles out *Super Boetium De Trinitate* q. 5, a. 1, ad 3—paired with *In I Anal. Post.* lect. 2, no. 5 and lect. 15—to resolve modern axiomatic controversies (notably Bertrand Russell's critique of *Elements* I.1) over mathematical existence. Hoenen observes that while continuous magnitude (*magnitudo*) is the fundamental presupposed subject-genus of geometry, determinate figures such as the equilateral triangle and the square function as secondary subjects whose non-contradictory mathematical existence cannot merely be assumed nominally, but must be proved through *quasi-operative* rational construction (*opus ipsius rationis*). For Hoenen, Aquinas's recognition of an interior constructive work within speculative mathematics explains how Euclidean postulates bridge pure theoretical contemplation and generative geometric synthesis without lapsing into pragmatism or conventionalism.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's isolation of mathematics as a speculative science possessing an immediate interior *opus rationis*—measuring, numbering, and constructing apart from sensible matter while remaining distinct from arbitrary human fabrication—captures the exact philosophical identity of the GEOMETOR ecosystem. In *geometor.model*, compass-and-straightedge operations are enacted as pure rational acts that do not approximate physical ink or pixels, but unfold necessary algebraic consequences latent within exact symbolic space. Simultaneously, Aquinas's account of subalternation in *ad 5*—wherein arithmetic and geometry supply the *propter quid* reasons for harmonic and astronomical phenomena—anticipates the architecture linking *geometor.model* to *geometor.divine* and *geometor.phyllotaxis*, where pure radical proportions such as the golden ratio provide the formal explanatory ground for harmonic ranges and natural botanical symmetries.

section_notes.heading: Commentary on Question V, Article 2
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Article 2 rests upon Aristotle's anti-Platonic polemic in *Metaphysics* I.6 (987a32–b10) and VII.7–11 (1033a24–1037a10), together with *Physics* II.2 and VIII.5–10 and *On the Soul* III.4 (429b10–22). Whereas Plato inferred from Cratylean sensory flux that universal definitions must refer to separate subsistent Forms, Aristotle distinguished concrete singulars (Socrates, *this* bronze sphere) from universal composite essences that include common matter (flesh and bones universally) while excluding individual material designation. Aquinas sharpens Aristotle's *Metaphysics* VII.10 distinction by forging his signature doctrine of *designated matter* (*materia signata*—matter subject to determinate spatial dimensions responsible for *hic et nunc* local position and individuation) as opposed to *undesignated* or *common matter* (*materia communis*), and by invoking *On the Soul* III.4 to explain our secondary knowledge of material singulars via intellectual *reflexio* mediated by the sensitive powers.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Two striking geometric principles animate Aquinas's argument in Article 2. First, in *co. 2*, local motion is identified as the primary motion presupposed by all physical change, and individuation in the mobile continuum is traced to *designated dimensions* (*dimensiones signatae*)—anticipating the way a concrete geometric diagram instantiates universal geometric ratios within particular chosen coordinates without restricting the theorem's universality to that singular placement. Second, in *ad 3*, Aquinas illustrates how natural philosophy reaches the immaterial First Mover as its extrinsic *terminus* through the classical Euclidean analogy of the point and the line (*Elements* I, Defs. 1 and 3: *A point is that which has no part*, and *The extremities of a line are points*): just as the endpoint terminates a continuous one-dimensional magnitude and stands in an essential relation to it without itself possessing linear extension, so an unextended principle terminates a causal series of motions without sharing mobile materiality.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *La théorie du jugement d'après St Thomas d'Aquin* (1946; 2nd ed. 1953) and Chapters II–III of *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954), Hoenen draws extensively upon Aquinas's analysis of universal *rationes* and reflective application (*q. 5, a. 2, co. 3* and *ad 4*) to explain how universal necessary science grasps concrete reality. Hoenen emphasizes that in Thomistic noetics the universal nature is neither a Platonic hypostasis nor a subjective nominalist label, but an objective formal structure (*ratio*) abstracted from *hic et nunc* designation in the pre-predicative phantasm. When the intellect judges, it uses this immobile *ratio* as a formal medium of knowing (*ut medio sciendi*) and reflects back upon the concrete data presented by the lower cognitive powers, thereby validating both the necessity of pure geometric theorems and their legitimate application to extended physical bodies.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's distinction between singular *designated dimensions* (*hic et nunc* coordinates) and universal intelligible *rationes*, together with his geometric analogy in *ad 3* of the indivisible point as the non-homogeneous *terminus* of a line, directly illuminates symbolic modeling in *geometor.model*. When a construction begins from two initial anchor points at coordinates (0, 0) and (1, 0), those chosen coordinates play the role of *designated dimensions* instantiating the construction, yet the algebraic and projective relationships uncovered across the resulting directed acyclic graph express universal *per se* geometric invariants wholly independent of scale, translation, or rotation. Likewise, in *geometor.model*, points arise not as tiny physical specks of extension, but as exact zero-dimensional algebraic limits (*termini*) generated at the intersections of lines and circles.

section_notes.heading: Commentary on Question V, Article 3
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: This article—universally recognized as Aquinas's masterwork on the philosophy of mathematics—weaves together *On the Soul* III.6 (430a26–b6, the *understanding of indivisibles* versus composition and division), *Physics* II.2 (193b31–35, *abstrahentium non est mendacium* and the contrast between *curvum* and *simum*), *Metaphysics* VII.10–11 (1036a9–12, *hyle noete* or *intelligible matter* as what is present in sensible things not insofar as they are sensible, such as mathematical objects), *Categories* 6 (5a15–37, quantity having *situs* or relative position of parts), and *Posterior Analytics* II.11 (94a28–34, the angle in a semicircle proved right from two half-right angles as a material-cause demonstration). Remarkably, Aquinas's autograph manuscripts in Vatican Latin MS 9850 reveal multiple painstaking drafts of this exact *responsio*, wherein he perfected the terminological triad of *separatio*, *abstractio formae*, and *abstractio totius* to supersede earlier Boethian and Avicennian accounts.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Every major structural feature of Euclid's *Elements* finds its philosophical warrant in Question V, Article 3. In *arg. 3* and *ad 3*, Aquinas addresses how the geometer numbers distinct straight lines of the same species to construct an equilateral triangle (*Elements* I.1) or a square (*Elements* I.46), grounding congruent multiplicity in *situs*—the order of parts intrinsic to dimensive quantity (*Categories* 6, mirrored in *Elements* I, Common Notion 4 on superposition and congruence). In *co. 4*, Aquinas contrasts *parts of the species* (the three bounding straight lines essential to a triangle in *Elements* I, Def. 19) with *parts of matter* (the accidental division of a circle into semicircles in *Elements* I, Def. 18). And in *arg. 4* and *ad 4*, he explains Aristotle's famous example corresponding to *Elements* III.31—that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle—by showing that decomposing a geometric whole into quantitative sub-angles argues not from physical matter, but from *intelligible matter*.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In Chapter IV of *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954, p. 131, fn. 2; cf. Chapter II on *ST* I, q. 85, a. 1, ad 2), Hoenen transcribes *Super Boetium De Trinitate* q. 5, a. 3, ad 3 verbatim as a cornerstone of geometric epistemology. Against Kant's claim that arithmetic and geometry require an *a priori* subjective form of pure sensibility to account for congruent multiplicity (such as distinct congruent triangles or enantiomorphs), Hoenen demonstrates from Aquinas's text that *materia intelligibilis*—dimensive quantity abstracted from sensible qualities by *abstractio formae* while retaining *situs* (the order of parts in homogeneous extension)—is objectively abstracted directly from sensible phantasms. Furthermore, Hoenen links Aquinas's twofold operation of the intellect (*co. 1*) to his own central thesis in *La théorie du jugement*: simple apprehension abstracts the nexus of quantitative features in *intelligible matter*, while judgment affirms its necessary formal necessity.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Question V, Article 3 provides the exact ontological charter for GEOMETOR's symbolic engine. In *geometor.model*, points, lines, and circles are stripped of all *sensible matter*—floating-point measurement noise, physical thickness, and material perturbation—through a computational realization of *abstraction of form*, while preserving *intelligible matter* and *situs*: distinct lines and circles of identical species are individuated and numbered precisely by their exact algebraic order and positional incidence within the plane, allowing multiple equilateral triangles and squares to be constructed and compared. Moreover, Aquinas's defense of geometric part-whole demonstrations in *intelligible matter* (*ad 4*, illustrated by the semicircle theorem of *Elements* III.31) mirrors how *geometor.divine* and *geometor.elements* analyze complex polygons and harmonic ranges through exact algebraic part-whole decompositions in SymPy.

section_notes.heading: Commentary on Question V, Article 4
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: In reconciling Aristotle's two characterizations of first philosophy—as the universal science of *being insofar as it is being* (*Metaphysics* IV.1, 1003a21) and as *theology* studying immobile, separable divine substance (*Metaphysics* VI.1, 1026a19; XII.6–10)—Aquinas resolves a celebrated tension debated by Alexander of Aphrodisias, Avicenna (*Liber de philosophia prima* I.1–2), and Averroes (*In I Phys.*, comm. 83). Avicenna had rightly insisted against Averroes that God cannot be the presupposed *subject* of metaphysics because God's existence is proved within metaphysics, not assumed at its outset; Aquinas adopts Avicenna's subject (*ens in quantum est ens*) while showing that God and the separate Intelligences enter metaphysics precisely as the universal causal principles of all being, thereby distinguishing philosophical metaphysics from Scriptural *sacra doctrina* (where divine realities self-revealed in faith constitute the proper subject itself) and refuting Avicebron's universal hylomorphism via Boethius's *De Hebdomadibus* distinction of *quod est* and *esse*.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Two vital mathematical contrasts sharpen Aquinas's metaphysical doctrine in Article 4. First, in *co. 1*, Aquinas contrasts subsistent causal principles with incomplete intrinsic principles such as *the unit of number and the point of a line* (*unitas numeri et punctus lineae*, corresponding to Euclid's *Elements* VII, Def. 1 and I, Def. 1): because point and unit are not complete natures subsisting apart from magnitude and multitude, they do not generate a separate science prior to geometry and arithmetic, but are treated solely within geometry and arithmetic as principles of their subject-genus. Second, in *arg. 7* and *ad 7* (following *Metaphysics* III.2, 996a21–35, where Aristippus mocked mathematics for ignoring the good and final causes), Aquinas explains why Euclidean demonstrations never argue from efficient or final causality: because mathematical figures are separated solely in consideration (*secundum considerationem tantum*), dynamic agency and teleology belong not to abstract figures as such, but only to real subsistent beings.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In the extensive Appendix to *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954) and Chapter X of *La théorie du jugement*, Hoenen explores how Thomistic epistemology ascends from the quidditative nexus of geometric essences to the metaphysical affirmation of *ipsum esse* and transcendental modes of being. Analyzing Aquinas's distinction in *q. 5, a. 4, co. 4* and *ad 5* between mathematical abstraction (whose objects can never exist apart from matter) and metaphysical *separatio* (which grasps *ens*, *substantia*, *potentia*, and *actus* as neutrally independent of matter *secundum esse*), Hoenen argues against rationalist essentialism—citing Gilson alongside Aquinas's *De Potentia* q. 7, a. 2, ad 9—that *ipsum esse* (*quo est* in *ad 4*) is the actuality of all acts, initially encountered in concrete sensible and kinetic judgments and purified through negative *separatio* without ever turning common being into a univocal quantitative genus.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's precision in *co. 1* and *ad 7* illuminates both the power and the principled boundaries of geometric formalization in GEOMETOR. Within *geometor.model*, points and unit segments function exactly as Aquinas describes *punctus lineae* and *unitas numeri*: not as isolated metaphysical substances, but as generative principles intrinsic to the constructive system of lines, circles, and algebraic ratios. Equally significant is Aquinas's explanation in *ad 7* of why mathematics excludes efficient and final causality in favor of pure formal necessity: in a constructive DAG within *geometor.elements* or *geometor.model*, ancestral dependencies represent timeless formal entailments rather than physical forces in time, even though the beauty and proportional harmony uncovered by *geometor.divine* invite philosophical reflection beyond pure geometry toward natural and metaphysical order.

section_notes.heading: Commentary on Question VI, Article 1
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expounding Boethius's famous methodological triad (*De Trinitate* c. 2: *in naturalibus rationabiliter, in mathematicis disciplinaliter, in divinis intellectualiter*), Aquinas synthesizes *Posterior Analytics* I.27 (87a31–37, arithmetic as more certain and prior to geometry, which exists *ex additione* by adding position to unit), *Physics* I.1 (184a16–21, proceeding from sensible effects better known to us toward causes better known by nature), *Metaphysics* II.3 (995a12–16, learning the mode of science before science itself, and demanding mathematical rigor only of immaterial subjects), Ptolemy's *Almagest* (I.1), Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy* (IV, pr. 6; V, pr. 4), and Pseudo-Dionysius's *On the Divine Names* (Ch. 7). He integrates these with the Neoplatonic-Scholastic method of *via resolutionis* (analysis back to simplest extrinsic or intrinsic principles) and *via compositionis vel inventionis* (synthesis descending from first principles to conclusions).
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's analysis of mathematical demonstration in *co. 3* and *co. 11–12* directly reflects classical Greek geometric practice from Euclid to Pappus. In *co. 3*, Aquinas notes that mathematics demonstrates solely through the formal cause (intrinsic definition), and remarkably anticipates an objection from Euclidean auxiliary constructions: when a geometer proves a property of a circle through an inscribed or circumscribed triangle or vice versa (as in *Elements* IV and XII.2), he does not invoke an extrinsic physical cause, because *in the circle the triangle exists potentially, and conversely*—echoing Aristotle's *Metaphysics* IX.9 (1051a21–33) on geometrical discovery actualizing latent divisions! Furthermore, Aquinas's coupling of *via resolutionis* and *via compositionis* in *co. 22* mirrors the classical geometric pair of *analysis* and *synthesis* codified in Pappus's *Collection* Book VII (*Treasury of Analysis*).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen explicitly cites *Super Boetium De Trinitate* q. 6, a. 1 in Chapter V of *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954, line 132: *both sciences—metaphysics and logic—are common, and in a certain way concerning the same subject*) while distinguishing *logica docens* from *logica utens* (*co. 1–2*): in building geometry, logic in use becomes the living form immanent within concrete mathematical demonstrations, governed by objective laws of being rather than arbitrary syntactic conventions. Moreover, in Chapters I, IV, and VII, Hoenen builds upon Aquinas's vindication of mathematics as *disciplinalis* par excellence (*co. 11–12* and *ad 14*, where mathematical reason *receives from the imagination*): geometry serves Aristotle and Aquinas as the *archetypus scientiae* precisely because its formal-cause demonstrations actualize latent nexus in imaginable extension with immediate, indubitable clarity.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's striking remark in *q. 6, a. 1, co. 3*—that when geometry demonstrates properties of a circle from a triangle or conversely, it does so because *the triangle exists potentially in the circle and conversely*—resonates profoundly with constructive discovery in *geometor.model*, *geometor.explorer*, and *geometor.divine*. Every step of a compass-and-straightedge construction in *geometor.model* actualizes points, segments, and polygons already latent *in potentia* within the algebraic field of the initial configuration; *geometor.divine* then performs a systematic *resolutio*, scanning the completed construction to uncover emergent golden sections and harmonic cross-ratios that flow by pure formal necessity from the underlying definitions, exemplifying Ptolemy's and Aquinas's *demonstration wrought by indubitable paths*.

section_notes.heading: Commentary on Question VI, Article 2
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Question VI, Article 2 brings Aquinas's theory of scientific judgment to completion by uniting *On the Soul* III.7–8 (431a16–b2, 432a8–14: the soul never understands without a *phantasm*, and phantasms stand to the intellective soul as sensible objects to sense), *On the Heavens* III.7 (306a5–17, where Aristotle rebukes the Platonists for forcing physical elements into geometric polyhedra in defiance of sensory observation, insisting that physical science must terminate at sensory appearance), *On the Soul* I.1 (403a12–16, alongside *Metaphysics* III.2, 997b35–998a4, refuting Protagoras's cavil that a straight ruler touches a bronze sphere across a sensible expanse rather than at a point), and Pseudo-Dionysius's *On the Divine Names* and *Mystical Theology* (the triplex via of causality, eminence, and negation).
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's concrete example in *co. 3*—that a mathematical straight line touches a sphere at a single indivisible point alone, whereas a physical ruler touches a material sphere along an extended patch—corresponds directly to Euclid's *Elements* III.16 (a straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity falls outside the circle and touches it at one point alone) extended stereometrically to the sphere (as in Theodosius's *Sphaerica* I.3). By distinguishing what external sense perceives in rough bronze or chalk from what constructive *imagination* exhibits under the governance of a *definitive notion* (*ratio diffinitiva*), Aquinas explains how Euclidean diagrams function in proof: the geometer never measures chalk thickness with empirical calipers (*ad sensum*), but judges exact point-incidence and tangency by terminating judgment at idealized spatial imagination (*ad imaginationem*).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Chapters III and IV of Hoenen's *De Noetica Geometriae* (1954) constitute an extended philosophical commentary on the exact doctrine of *q. 6, a. 2, co. 3* and *ad 6*. Examining Aristotle's and Aquinas's response to Protagoras on tangent lines and angle sums (*In III Metaph.* lect. 7, no. 416; *In I Anal. Post.* lect. 42, no. 7; *ST* I, q. 84, a. 6–7), Hoenen demonstrates how *terminari ad imaginationem* avoids both empiricist skepticism (which denies exact points and lines because sensation is coarse) and Platonic or Hilbertian formalism (which severs geometry from spatial intuition altogether). Because the *phantasm* remains a *permanent foundation* (*permanens fundamentum*, *ad 6*) illuminated by the agent intellect, the geometer inspects within imaginative extension itself the exact indivisibility of limits and necessary incidence relations, verifying universal geometric judgments in constructive intuition.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's twin theses in Question VI, Article 2—that the *phantasm* abides as a *permanent foundation* (*permanens fundamentum*) of intellectual insight, and that mathematical judgment *terminates at the imagination* (*terminari ad imaginationem*) rather than at coarse empirical sensation—define the exact synergy between *geometor.model* and *geometor.explorer*. Whereas floating-point CAD or dynamic geometry software reduces tangency and intersection to numerical pixel tolerances (*ad sensum*, where a tangent line and circle may blur or miss due to rounding error), *geometor.model* adjudicates every incidence according to its exact *definitive notion* in SymPy symbolic algebra—verifying, just as Aquinas writes in *co. 3*, that a tangent line meets a circle at a single exact algebraic point—while *geometor.explorer* renders luminous SVG diagrams and animations as precision visual *phantasms* in which the human intellect directly inspects and contemplates the intelligible structure of the construction.
